scope.completeness: Not a manual handbook-image extraction or exhaustive per-card semantic audit; misses and false positives are possible. Sources, currentness and accuracy remain subject to independent review.

needs.title: Traffic and pedestrian signals

source_cards.front: What are three forms of traffic control?
source_cards.back: Traffic signals, roadside signs and pavement markings are forms of traffic control.

source_cards.front: What safety condition applies even with a green light?
source_cards.back: A green traffic light allows travel only when proceeding is safe.

source_cards.front: Where are green and red placed relative to yellow in a usual vertical signal?
source_cards.back: In the usual vertical traffic signal, green is below yellow and red is above yellow.

source_cards.front: What yielding qualification remains when entering on steady green?
source_cards.back: A steady green light allows entry into the intersection while required yielding duties still apply.

source_cards.front: What must a stopped driver wait for after receiving green?
source_cards.back: When a stopped driver receives a green light, traffic already crossing must clear before the driver moves.

source_cards.front: Which direction does a green arrow authorize?
source_cards.back: A green arrow authorizes a turn in its indicated direction.

source_cards.front: Who has priority when you turn left on a steady green light?
source_cards.back: A left turn on a steady green light is permitted only when safe, with oncoming traffic having priority.

source_cards.front: What does steady yellow mean when stopping is safe?
source_cards.back: A steady yellow light warns of the coming red light and requires stopping when stopping is safe.

source_cards.front: How should a driver respond to flashing yellow?
source_cards.back: A flashing yellow light calls for reduced speed and cautious travel.

source_cards.front: What change does a yellow arrow signal and what preparation follows?
source_cards.back: A yellow arrow ends protected turning time; if turning in its direction, prepare to stop and yield to oncoming traffic before turning.

source_cards.front: What does a steady red light require?
source_cards.back: A steady red light requires a stop.

source_cards.front: What does a bright blinking light inside a red signal emphasize?
source_cards.back: A bright blinking light located inside a red signal is an added warning that the red light requires stopping.

source_cards.front: What does flashing red require before proceeding?
source_cards.back: A flashing red signal requires the same complete stop as a stop sign, followed by travel only when safe.

source_cards.front: What does a red arrow prohibit while it remains red?
source_cards.back: A red arrow requires stopping and forbids movement in its direction while it remains red.

source_cards.front: What signal change allows movement after a red arrow?
source_cards.back: Movement following a red arrow may begin after it goes out and a green arrow or green light appears.

needs.title: Railroad crossing approaches and tracks

source_cards.front: What does the handbook say about racing trains to a crossing?
source_cards.back: Do not race a train to a railroad crossing.

source_cards.front: What does the handbook say about space beyond railroad tracks?
source_cards.back: Enter a railroad crossing only when the space beyond can hold your entire vehicle without stopping on the tracks.

source_cards.front: What does the handbook say about the circular advance railroad warning?
source_cards.back: A circular yellow sign carrying an X and the letters RR warns of a railroad crossing ahead.

source_cards.front: What does the handbook say about flashing railroad warning lights?
source_cards.back: Stop when the alternating lights at a railroad crossing flash for an approaching train.

source_cards.front: What does the handbook say about required stops before railroad crossings?
source_cards.back: School buses, taxis and other for-hire vehicles carrying passengers, and trucks transporting dangerous materials must stop at least fifteen feet before a railroad crossing.

source_cards.front: What does the handbook say about the railroad crossbuck description?
source_cards.back: A railroad crossbuck is white and X-shaped and bears the words Railroad Crossing.

source_cards.front: What does the handbook say about the stop-sign description?
source_cards.back: A stop sign is a red octagon bearing white lettering.

source_cards.front: What does the handbook say about the required stop-sign stopping position?
source_cards.back: At a stop sign, stop completely at the stop line if one is present, or at the sign if no line is provided.

source_cards.front: What does the handbook say about safe travel after a stop?
source_cards.back: After stopping at a stop sign, wait for crossing vehicles and pedestrians to clear, then move only when safe.

source_cards.front: What does the handbook say about the yield-sign description?
source_cards.back: A yield sign is a red-and-white triangle with its point facing downward.

source_cards.front: What does the handbook say about yield-sign approach and traffic priority?
source_cards.back: At a yield sign, reduce speed and give priority to traffic in the intersection or on the road being entered.

source_cards.front: What does the handbook say about yield-sign lettering color?
source_cards.back: The downward-pointing red-and-white yield sign has red lettering.

source_cards.front: What does the handbook say about service-sign shapes?

source_cards.back: Pavement markings can designate pedestrian crossings and the stopping position for a sign or signal.

source_cards.front: What does the handbook say about white lines and traffic direction?
source_cards.back: White lane lines separate streams of traffic moving the same way.

source_cards.front: What does the handbook say about safe broken-white lane changes?
source_cards.back: A broken white lane line allows a lane change after checking that the movement is safe.

source_cards.front: What does the handbook say about the solid-white lane-change qualification?
source_cards.back: A solid white lane line calls for staying in the lane unless a special circumstance requires a change.

source_cards.front: What does the handbook say about stopping before lines or crosswalks?
source_cards.back: For a stop required by a sign or signal, stop before the vehicle reaches the stop line or crosswalk.

source_cards.front: What does the handbook say about yellow lines and opposing traffic?
source_cards.back: Yellow lane lines separate vehicles moving toward each other.

source_cards.front: What does the handbook say about safe broken-yellow passing?
source_cards.back: A broken yellow center line permits passing when the maneuver is safe.

source_cards.front: What does the handbook say about the solid side of paired lines?
source_cards.back: With a paired solid and broken yellow center line, a driver on the solid-line side may not pass.

source_cards.front: What does the handbook say about the broken side of paired lines?
source_cards.back: With a paired solid and broken yellow center line, a driver beside the broken line may pass when safe.

source_cards.front: What does the handbook say about double solid yellow lines?
source_cards.back: A double solid yellow center line prohibits passing from either side.

source_cards.front: What does the handbook say about safe driveway turns across yellow?
source_cards.back: A driver may cross a solid yellow line to enter a driveway when the turn is safe.

source_cards.front: What does the handbook say about shared-middle-lane boundary markings?
source_cards.back: A shared middle lane is bounded on each side by a solid yellow line paired with a broken yellow line.

source_cards.front: What does the handbook say about reversible-lane yellow markings?
source_cards.back: Reversible lanes are commonly marked by paired broken yellow lines.
